1.	What was envisaged in the Nepean point project, with whom did the plan originate, and what preparatory work thereon has been done to date?
2.	Who presently opposes this project and for what reason?
Answer: 1. The primary purpose of the Nepean point project was the provision of a suitable repository for the books of remembrance commemorating those Canadians who gave their lives in the Nile expedition and the South African war, world war II and the Korean campaign. The need for such a repository became apparent in 1954, as the world war II book was nearing completion, and cabinet authorized the then minister of veterans affairs, Hon. Hugues Lapointe, to appoint an advisory committee to study this matter and make recommendations.

The committee worked on the premise that the world war II book should have a permanent resting place comparable in artistic development, dignity and general atmosphere to the memorial chamber in the peace tower, which is the permanent repository of the world war I book of remembrance.
After studying existing and proposed government buildings, the committee concluded that a suitable chamber could not be constructed in any of them and it recommended the erection of a shrine of remembrance for this purpose on Nepean point.
In 1956 the minister announced in the house that the recommendation of the committee had been accepted by the government, and that the minister of public works had been instructed to proceed with the design of an appropriate building. Consultants were appointed and produced a number of preliminary designs. The selected design, along with a model, was submitted to the advisory committee on design of the national capital commission who requested a revision to reduce the size of the building and the government directed that the total cost must be lower. The consultants later produced such a revision. Preliminary drawings and elevations and a revised model of the project have been prepared but have not been submitted to the national capital commission.
Subsequent governments confirmed the original decision to construct a shrine and in February, 1963 it was announced that a design had been approved in principle. In September the Prime Minister confirmed that this government had decided to proceed with the project. Some controversy, however, had been developing on the need or the desirability of proceeding with the planning and in October the Minister of Veterans Affairs announced that action would be deferred until a careful review and further study of the project had been completed. No working drawings or specifications of the shrine have been prepared and no work is proceeding at the present time.
In 1955 the Royal Canadian Legion recommended the construction of a cenotaph, not identified with any war, which would become the focal point for future national remembrance and similar services. This recommendation was also referred to the advisory committee which recommended, in due course, that such a cenotaph be erected on Nepean point also, after the razing of the old printing bureau building.
This recommendation, also, was accepted by the government but no design for such a cenotaph has been prepared to date.

subtopic: NEWS COVERAGE FOR ARMED FORCES ABROAD
NEWS COVERAGE FOR ARMED FORCES ABROAD
speechtext:
Has the government received any representations to the effect that members of the various branches of the armed forces in Europe receive almost no Canadian news coverage of events taking place in Canada and, if so, does the government have any plans to remedy this situation and what is the nature of such plans?
Answer: No such representations have been received, in so far as national defence is concerned. At the present time, Canadian news is broadcast over Radio Canadian Army Europe five times daily, Monday through Friday, with additional broadcasts on Saturday and Sunday. The R.C.A.F. No. 1 air division operates radio stations at each of its five bases. News is broadcast four to five times daily with additional coverage on Sundays. In addition, the Canadian press provides a daily newscript, Monday through Saturday, which is transmitted over the armed forces telecommunication system each night and rebroadcast over local stations. Canadian newspapers are provided through non-public funds.
News transmissions from Canada by short wave are affected by electronic and atmospheric conditions and are limited by the capability of the transmitter and receiver system on both sides of the Atlantic. As a result, the transmission reception and rebroadcast of Canadian news has never been entirely satisfactory. This has been a matter of discussion between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Department of External Affairs and the Department of National Defence.

subtopic: J. D. MCLEOD, NORTHERN AFFAIRS  QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
(a) Mr. McLeod graduated in 1939 with the degree of B.A.Sc. in civil engineering from the University of British Columbia. He is a member of the association of professional engineers of the province of Ontario, a member of the engineering institute of Canada, and a member of the American geophysical union.
(b) Mr. McLeod has 21 years of service with the water resources branch and its predecessors. The branch formerly was known as the water resources division and prior to that as the dominion water and power bureau. During this service his duties have included:
(i)	Junior hydraulic engineer on field and office surveys in connection with the bureau streamflow and water level program in British Columbia and the Yukon Territory.

(vi)	Senior hydraulic engineer and chief of the international waterways section of the water resources division; responsible for division studies, reports and data on international water problems on the Columbia, Waterton, Belly, Souris, Red and Saint John river systems. These studies, reports and data included both those undertaken solely by the division and those undertaken in co-operation with other government agencies, consulting engineers and representatives of private corporations, among them the corps of engineers, United States army; United States bureau of reclamation; the federal power commission (United States); The Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario; Manitoba hydro; The New Brunswick Electric Power Commission; B.C. Power Commission (now B.C. Hydro); Montreal Engineering Company Limited; Shawinigan Engineering Company Limited; H.G. Acres Company Limited; Crippen-Wright Engineering Limited; and the national research council.
(vii)	Assistant chief of the water resources division with continuing responsibility for international water problems as outlined in
(vi)	above and additional responsibilities as member or secretary of various international engineering boards established by the international joint commission to investigate these problems as well as with responsibility for numerous other division functions. Appointed member for Canada of the Canadian and international control boards responsible for the regulation of storage in the Winnipeg river system in Ontario and Minnesota and in lake Memphremagog in Quebec and Vermont.
(viii)	Chief of the water resources division and hence responsible for all division activities and functions; associated responsibilities included those on international water problems as outlined in (vii) above.
(ix)	Chief engineer of the water resources branch; responsible for all activities and functions of the branch operations division; associated responsibilities included those on international water problems as outlined in (vii) above.
(x)	Acting director, water resources branch; responsible for all branch activities and functions including associated responsibilities on international water problems as outlined in
(vii)	above.
(c)	In the course of his duties in the water resources branch and its predecessors Mr. McLeod has participated actively in studies of international water matters, including their national aspects both for the department and for the Department of External Affairs, as well as for the international joint commission. Many of these studies have included the performance of detailed investigations, planning,

development of preliminary designs, performance of flowage appraisal surveys, preparation of estimates, programming and performance of studies to determine most effective system power operation and review of economic factors involved in the generation of hydroelectric power as well as in other water uses. speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DELAY IN EXECUTION OF WARRANT AGAINST HAL BANKS
speechtext:
It is a well established rule that letters and other communications between ministers and officials, or between officials, and memoranda and records relating to conversations between ministers and officials, or between officials, are privileged and cannot be produced. I therefore cannot agree to produce any such material which might exist.
I have in mind a number of motions which I made when I was on the other side of the house, one in particular which was refused and which I have no right to go into at this time, and another which was made by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asking for production of the "Canadian Economic Outlook" for 1958, to which the former prime minister replied by stating the information was confidential and could not be produced. If the Leader of the Opposition is not willing to accept this, or is not willing to withdraw his motion, my suggestion is that the motion be transferred for debate at a later date.

subtopic: DELAY IN EXECUTION OF WARRANT AGAINST HAL BANKS
speechtext:
I do not accept the suggestion of the minister that this is privileged. The words of the warrant are mandatory and do not permit of interference by the Minister of Justice. In ordinary circumstances I would agree that letters, memoranda or verbal instructions of the kind to which the hon. gentleman has referred would not be producible when the minister acts according to law; but in the wording of the warrant, form 7, the following appears:	"This is,
therefore, to command you-" that is, the peace officer

 "in Her Majesty's name forthwith to arrest the accused".
This being so, the action admittedly taken by the Minister of Justice cannot be justified, and when he acts above the law what he does must be producible; otherwise lawlessness would be condoned and encouraged.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DELAY IN EXECUTION OF WARRANT AGAINST HAL BANKS
speechtext:

I would simply say to the right hon. gentleman that if he wants this matter placed on the order paper for debate I am quite satisfied, and I hope to be able to bring forward instances, when he was in office, of a position being taken identical with that taken by the Minister of Justice on this occasion.

subsubtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL  STATEMENT ON RIOTS
speechtext:
On Monday the hon. member for Vancouver East asked me whether the commissioner of penitentiaries had completed his investigation into the riots at St. Vincent de Paul and the alleged attacks by guards on the alleged leaders of the riots. A summary of the findings and recommendations of the commission of inquiry convened by the commissioner of penitentiaries under the Penitentiary Act in respect of the riots was tabled in the house in June last.
With respect to the question of alleged attacks by guards on the alleged leaders of the riots, I presume that the hon. member is referring to the case of Alvin Gunn. On October 29 last I tabled a statement with respect to this case, and it was printed in Hansard at page 4134. This investigation, which was limited in scope, was conducted by the regional director of penitentiaries over a two day period, and evidence was not taken under oath.
In the light of the findings of that inquiry the commissioner of penitentiaries, acting pursuant to the powers that he has under the Penitentiary Act, appointed a legal officer of the Department of Justice, Mr. Louis Philippe Landry, as a commissioner to inquire into and report upon the alleged physical abuse used against Gunn. Mr. Landry, acting under his powers to subpoena witnesses and take evidence under oath, conducted an inquiry accordingly and reported his findings to the commissioner. The finding was that Alvin Gunn had been severely beaten by eight penitentiary officers and that the beating was not necessary under the circumstances.
At the time of Mr. Landry's inquiry five of the officers had already resigned or were under suspension for other reasons. The remaining three officers were charged before a disciplinary board under the penitentiary regulations with the offence of having used excessive force against Gunn. The board found one of them guilty and recommended a severe reprimand. The board concluded that there was not sufficient evidence to justify conviction of the remaining two officers.

speakeroldname: Hon. Maurice Lamonlagne (President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
There are a number of different subjects which might properly be discussed as we consider the estimates of the privy council. So as to have a more orderly discussion, I propose to hon. members that we defer consideration of the estimates of the emergency measures organization until the very end of our deliberations. At that time, the Minister of Industry, who is now responsible for this organization, will take over. I would also suggest that the general discussion on centennial projects and programs be postponed until we reach the vote concerning the centennial administration. If this procedure is acceptable-and I hope it will be, for it will make for a much more orderly discussion, as I have suggested-it would perhaps be convenient for me to say a few words at this point, about the bureau of government organization which forms part of the privy council office and about the progress that has been achieved in implementing the recommendations of the royal commission on government organization, generally referred to as the Glassco commission.
The first volume of the reports of the commission appeared in September, 1962. Since then four additional volumes have been published. Volume 5 appeared in May of this year. The commission has now discharged its mandate. Its staff of experts and consultants, combined with officers seconded to it from within the public service, has now been disbanded.
I should like to take advantage of the opportunity presented by this discussion of the estimates to express the thanks of the government and of the people of Canada to the commissioners and to all those who were associated with them in their monumental study of the structure and organization of the government of Canada in all its many forms. The present government holds the view that the findings and the recommendations of the commissioners deserve the most serious and careful study.
There is, in the view of the government, much in the report of the commissioners that will, if carried into effect, achieve one of the commission's prime objectives as stated in its terms of reference, namely "to provide efficiency, economy and improved service in the dispatch of public business". At the same

Supply-Privy Council time, it must be added that there will inevitably be some recommendations which can only be accepted and implemented with suitable modifications, and others which may not be acceptable at all.
It was for the purpose of facilitating the detailed study and appraisal of the commission's numerous recommendations, about 300 in all, that the bureau of government organization was established by the preceding administration in the privy council office. The bureau was established in January of this year just prior to the publication of volume 3 of the commission's reports. It has continued to function actively throughout the year and the first major results of its work were seen in the list of 68 approved recommendations which I tabled in the house on November 5 last. If we add to this list the half dozen or more recommendations formally accepted and approved by the previous administration we can say that something like 25 per cent of the formal recommendations made by the Glassco commission in its five volumes, containing 24 reports, have now been formally approved by the government.
I should add immediately with reference to the statement I have just made that I recognize the impossibility of judging the progress made in implementing the commission's findings simply by reference to the percentage of recommendations that have been approved. The 75 or more formal recommendations which have been accepted to date are not in all cases to be considered among the most important of the commission's recommendations. Many of the more fundamental and far reaching proposals still remain to be assessed and decided. Indeed, many of the most important proposals of the commission are not set out as formal recommendations at all. Instead they are embodied in the text of the reports themselves, not as formal recommendations but explicitly or implicitly as part of the argument of the commissioners. I cite as instances of my point report No. 1 entitled, "A Plan For Management", the separate report of commissioner Therrien on bilingualism in the public service, and report No. 19 on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Not one of these three reports contains a single formal recommendation. One has to look to the text of the reports themselves and to the argument advanced in the text to determine what criticisms are offered concerning the present arrangements and what changes, by inference if not directly, are advocated.
This is why I say that the findings of the commissioners, both their formal recommendations and the implications of their criticisms and their observations on a wide variety of governmental activities, must be studied actively and with the greatest care in order
[Mr. Lamontaene.l

to determine the full implications of the changes which are proposed in the interests of improved and more effective service to the taxpaying public.
I should like now to direct the committee's attention to a number of major questions of principle to which the Glassco commission addressed itself, since it is only by so doing that we will be able to place in proper perspective the recommendations which the commissioners made and which the government has been considering. Perhaps the most important of these general questions has to do with the degree of concentration or delegation of authority that is to be sought in a service as large, as varied and as far-flung as is the federal public service. By its very nature the federal administration must be widely dispersed and highly decentralized in physical and geographical terms. That is not only highly desirable but entirely unavoidable in a country as vast as Canada.
We have also accepted in our governmental structure over the years a high degree of decentralization by departments and agencies. The proof of this is seen in the number of departments which have been created over the years and in the even larger number of independent and quasi-independent agencies, including crown corporations, which have been established by parliamentary action both in the pre-war and especially in the post-war years.
In another sense, however, with respect to authority for decision making there has been a lesser degree of decentralization than one might imagine if one were to judge solely by the appearances of geographical and departmental decentralization as applied to operations. So far as the basic authority and responsibility with respect to financial and personnel management are concerned, these have not been decentralized with respect to departments to anything like the same extent that they have been in the case of crown corporations or other agencies. For a good many years now, since 1918 or earlier in respect of personnel matters and since 1932 in respect of financial agencies, the civil service commission, the treasury board and the comptroller of the treasury have exercised detailed control over the personnel and financial activities of individual departments to an extent far beyond that which the Glassco commission considers necessary for the effective operations of the departments or for the proper safeguarding of the public interest.
The commissioners point out, for example, that under the provisions of the Civil Service Act it is the civil service commission which recruits, selects, promotes, transfers and

carries out most of the other important elements of the personnel function affecting the careers of the classified civil servant in a government department. It is the civil service commission, together with the treasury board, which deals with matters affecting establishments, classifications and reclassifications. It is the treasury board which in the final analysis deals with pay determination. In fact, very few of the decisions in the personnel field affecting the work performance, the careers and the effective deployment of the members of the civil service can legally be taken by the departments which, nominally at least, employ, direct and supervise the civil servants whose services they use to discharge the department's responsibilities.
The reasons which have led to the concentration of authority and responsibility in respect of personnel matters in the hands of the civil service commission and in the treasury board are of course well known, and have their roots in the early history of government in this country. While recognizing these historical factors, the Glassco commission concludes none the less that the removal of authority, responsibility and accountability from departments for personnel management has gone too far; that the departments have become weakened thereby; and that this has led to a degree of dependence by departments on the central control agencies, which is not healthy or conducive to sound concepts of organization or management. Where responsibility is too widely dispersed-where it is scattered, fragmented and shared by too many units of administration-it becomes almost impossible to fix or to pinpoint responsibility. By the same token it becomes more difficult to hold any one unit or authority accountable for the consequences of decisions which are taken.
The Glassco commission compares the position of the government departments and of the civil service in this respect, with the much greater concentration of authority, responsibility and accountability on line management that is found in private industry, and equally in the crown corporations and independent agencies. The commissioners ask, in this connection, what is so different about the position of 133,000 classified civil servants -and about the calibre and quality of departmental management-that they have to be treated so differently from employees in private industry, and so differently also from the much larger numbers of crown employees employed outside the confines of the Civil Service Act?
The conclusion of the commissioners is that the high degree of detailed and centralized control over individual personnel management decisions presently exercised by the
Supply-Privy Council civil service commission and by the treasury board is both unnecessary, and in fact detrimental to efficient administration. It recommends that central control continue to be exercised through the laying down of broad policies, directives, principles and guide lines through the treasury board; that the role of the civil service commission be substantially altered with the removal of many aspects of personnel administration from its jurisdiction and a strengthening of its role as an independent agency for the safeguarding of the merit system; and that departments be given greater responsibility for making the detailed individual personnel decisions affecting the employees of their respective departments, but always within the policy guide lines established by the central management authority, that is, the treasury board.
When we turn to the area of financial management, and to the relationship between the comptroller of the treasury and the treasury board with departmental managements, the commissioners present to us a similar picture. Under the Financial Administration Act the comptroller of the treasury must pre-audit every proposed payment of every department of government. Should the comptroller's view of the legality of the proposed payment, or of the eligibility of the proposed payee to receive the payment conflict with the view of the administering department, such disagreement can only be resolved by the decision of the treasury board. Such a system involves, in the view of the commissioners, an undesirable degree of protection, leading to dependence on the comptroller, for departments; inevitable duplication between the work of departments which must make the initial decision, and the comptroller, who must confirm or reject it; and excessive involvement of the treasury board in a large number of individual decisions when its primary concern and preoccupation should be with broad policy matters.
The full measure of the extent to which the responsibility for decision making has been shifted from departmental management to the central management authority of the treasury board can be seen from the table shown on page 131 of volume 1 of the Glassco report, which shows that in 1960 almost
16,000	submissions were made by departments and agencies to the treasury board seeking authority to make decisions. The number of management decisions, initiated by departments in the personnel field, or in the proposed authorization of money payments which require the sanction of the civil service commission or the comptroller of the treasury, is vastly in excess of the questions submitted for decision to the treasury board

Supply-Privy Council itself. In all three areas, the view of the Glassco commission is that the vast majority of these individual decisions on detailed points can and should be taken by departmental management within the framework of broad policy guide lines established by the treasury board or other central control agencies. In other words, the central control agencies should exercise control through policy formulation, and through a method of supervision which endeavours to assess the over-all effectiveness with which policies are carried out. If this viewpoint is accepted, it means in the view of the commissioners that the central control agencies concentrate on policy formulation, and disengage from detailed decision making with which they are so greatly overburdened at the present time. Departments, on the other hand, within the framework of the policies laid down for them to follow, would have the responsibility for making their own decisions, would not be excessively protected from the consequences of their own carelessness and mistakes as they are at present, and would be held accountable for the results, whether good or bad, which flow from their decisions.
At this point, the question can quite properly be asked: what is the government's attitude to the commission's point of view on this important question of financial management and control? Does the government subscribe to the philosophy of personnel and financial management outlined in the Glassco report?
The answer to this perfectly proper question must, of course, be a qualified one. By and large, however, the government's view on the score of financial management is indicated by the fact that it has accepted, in the list which I tabled on November 5 last, the recommendation set out at page 105 in volume 1, of the report that "departments and agencies be given a greater measure of financial authority and be held correspondingly accountable for the effective management of the financial resources placed at their disposal."
I should perhaps draw attention to an important difference between the recommendation as it appears in the commission's report and the form in which I have indicated the government's acceptance.
The report refers to departments being given "the necessary financial authority"; the recommendation as accepted by the government calls for departments to be given a greater measure of financial authority. This distinction is an important one. The government, in other words, is accepting and moving in the direction which the commission has recommended, that is to say, the direction of
IMr. Lamontagne.]
greater departmental management control, responsibility and accountability for its own administration.
The government has not yet, however, made a final determination as to how far it is prepared to go along the lines recommended by Glassco, nor is it prepared as yet to say that it will go the entire distance advocated by the commission. That is why it has to date indicated its acceptance of only 16 of the 27 recommendations contained in the financial management report. The remaining 11 have not been rejected; they have merely been reserved for more detailed study.
I should perhaps at this point refer to another step which we have decided to take in the process of testing the validity of the Glassco commission's recommendations on financial management in advance of their actual implementation. Members of the public accounts committee have already been advised of a number of feasibility studies which have been arranged to test the applicability of the commission's recommendations on financial management in the day to day administration of four separate departments. The departments engaged in these feasibility studies are the departments of agriculture, northern affairs and national resources, transport, and veterans affairs. In the case of northern affairs the study extends beyond questions of financial management to include the Glassco recommendations on personnel management and paperwork and systems management as well. Each of these four departments has retained the services of a management consultant to assist in working out the changes in departmental organization structure and procedures which would be required to implement fully all the Glassco recommendations in the fields mentioned.
These studies, which will take six months to complete, will cover not only the recommendations in the fields of financial management which the government has already accepted, but also those which have not as yet been decided. We hope and expect that out of the experience of these four departments we will be able to determine the extent to which it is sound and practicable to apply the commission's recommendations on financial and personnel management, etc., to the service as a whole.
My remarks to this point, Mr. Chairman, have related principally to the recommendations contained in the first volume of the Glassco commission's reports. Here the principal issue has been the division of responsibility between the central control agencies, treasury board, the civil service commission and the comptroller of the treasury on the one hand, and the departments on the other.

The commission comes down in favour of a substantial shift of management responsibilities on matters of detail to the departments.
There is one other issue of major importance raised by the commissioners in their very first report entitled "A Plan for Management". That has to do with the proposed relocation and reconstitution of treasury board, and the designation of a minister as the full-time president of treasury board. The principal reason advanced for this proposal by the commission is that the Minister of Finance, because of his other preoccupations and responsibilities has, in fact been unable for a number of years now to devote an adequate amount of time and attention to his duties as the chairman of treasury board. The commission expresses the view that if the trends of recent years continue there will be an increasing danger that the really effective control of treasury board decisions will come to rest increasingly with the staff of treasury board rather than with the ministers who make up treasury board itself. The commission therefore recommends that a full-time minister be named to preside over the work of the board, that the board itself be recognized effectively in its constitutional role as a committee of the privy council, and that in conformity with this concept of its role the staff of the board be reconstituted as an integral part of the privy council office, instead of the Department of Finance to which it presently belongs.
It is clear that this recommendation of the commission is one of fundamental importance to the future role and function of treasury board, and to the discharge of its responsibilities as the central management authority of the government itself. The existing arrangement whereby the Minister of Finance serves also as chairman of treasury board goes back to early days of confederation. The committee can be assured that the government is giving the most careful consideration to these important recommendations of the commission, but it may be some weeks yet before it is in a position to announce a definite decision one way or the other.
I have concentrated my remarks in large part, Mr. Chairman, on the reports contained in volume 1 of the commission's work, partly because we have had a longer period of time in which to study these reports, but more importantly because they deal with principles and problems which affect the functioning of the public service as a whole. I expect that within the next few months we will complete very largely our consideration of the important issues raised by the reports contained in volume 1, and that by the time
Supply-Privy Council this committee is called upon to consider the 1964-65 estimates of the bureau of government organization I will be in a position to present to the committee a report on the government's decisions with respect to the questions still outstanding. As the work on volume 1 approaches completion, we are turning our attention increasingly to the reports contained in the later volumes. The list of approved recommendations which I tabled on November 5 covers, in fact, a variety of matters contained in volumes 2 and 3, but does not touch volumes 4 and 5. These later reports are now receiving our detailed attention.
I should like to mention a particular group of recommendations, relating to report No. 6 on purchasing and supply, which the government has already announced its intention to implement. These recommendations call for the conversion of the Department of Defence Production into a department of supply, which will serve as the central procurement agency for most, if not all, departments and agencies of the federal government. As the committee knows, the Department of Defence Production already acts as the procurement agency for the defence department and the armed forces, whose combined requirements exceed by two or three times, in dollar value, all the procurement requirements of all the civilian departments and agencies of the government. The logic of the recommendation to establish a common procurement agency is therefore difficult to argue against. The Department of Defence Production has therefore been authorized to proceed by orderly stages, to the establishment of a central procurement agency to serve the common needs of all departments and functions of the federal government.
The first stage of this will consist of-

Supply-Privy Council Some commentators on the work of the Glassco commission have contended that the purchasing and supply recommendations, and others, contained in other reports throughout the second and subsequent volume, run directly counter to the principal recommendations contained in volume 1. Volume 1 would decentralize authority and control for detailed decision-making to departments. Volume 2 in the report on purchasing and supply would take the procurement function from the departments and centralize it in a common procurement agency. Is there a contradiction here? In the view of the government there is no contradiction. Under the arrangements proposed, the procurement authority and control will continue to rest with the individual departments and agencies. The departments will continue to decide what they need, what specifications should be laid down, what quantity and quality should be stipulated, what requisitions should issue, and so on. The departments, after all, are the ones which will be accountable for the expenditures of the funds voted by parliament. The new department of supply, on the other hand, will act solely as the agent of the requisitioning department, in a service not in a control capacity. It will be the task of the treasury board, as the central management agency of the government and the over-all policy making authority in this field, to ensure that the individual departments and agencies conform to the government's broad policy directives in the requisitions which they issue for the central procurement agency to fill. The control or supervision of departmental action will in no way be a function of the central procurement agency. If this principle is maintained, there will clearly be no conflict between the principles advocated by the commission and adopted by the government with respect to central procurement and those which favour a larger measure of departmental responsibility as set out in volume 1. Mr. Chairman, my last remarks on the recommendations of the Glassco commission, are related to the problem of bilingualism in the civil service. The commission submitted, in that field, five recommendations which have already been approved by the government and which we are now implementing.
Here are these recommendations:
1.	That the federal government adopt active measures to develop bilingual capacities among its employees on a selective basis.
2.	That the government intensify its efforts to attract and retain more of the highly-qualified young people of French Canada capable of advancement to senior ranks.


3.	That consideration be given to a review of the classification, remuneration, and career opportunities for translators throughout the public service.
4.	That steps be taken to attract more bilingual information officers to the public service.
5.	That, in every department and agency, full bilingualism be made a mandatory qualification for at least one of the top positions in the information service unit.
I must stress the fact that these recommendations are formal proposals, emanating from the commission as a body. They are not part of the minority report of Mr. Therrien, that I have already mentioned. Although Mr. Therrien in his report does not make any formal recommendations, he makes some very important and useful remarks on the subject of bilingualism in the federal administration. Mr. Therrien has explained most clearly the various aspects of a situation which has always existed but with which we cannot put up. We all know that it has to be corrected, improved.
It is partly for that reason that the government decided to set up a royal commission of inquiry on bilingualism and bicul-turalism.
However, the federal government felt that it should not wait for the commission's report to act. As early as last May, a special cabinet committee was established to look after administrative reform and bilingualism. I have the honour of being its chairman. As its first task, the committee has decided to define more clearly the objectives of the government regarding federal administration.
We have set ourselves the three following aims:
1.	To put in theory and practice, French and English on an equal footing for all public relations of the federal authorities. In practice, for external written or oral communications, the preference of the citizen would determine the language to be used.
2.	To establish a similar policy concerning internal communications within the civil service. Thus, correspondence and other written communications could be in English or in French, according to the writer's choice. A similar system should finally be set up for oral communications. Handbooks, general instructions and circulars would be published in both languages.
3.	To intensify the efforts being made to recruit a greater number of civil servants from French Canada and, to this end, to revise if need be, the competition system and recruiting methods.
In order to assist the government in reaching those objectives, an interdepartmental committee made up of officials representing the main departments and the crown corporations has also been established. This committee has been given the task of submitting

as soon as possible concrete recommendations on the following aspects of a general program.
1.	The nature and organization of French and English classes within the public service, for government officials as well as for other employees. The committee has already submitted a report on the matter and the government has approved a plan which is to be carried out, on an experimental basis, by the civil service commission and which will be used to determine the contents of a comprehensive program we expect to launch in 1964.
2.	The suitable measures to adopt to recruiting, training, promotion and assignment of employees, so as to better meet the requirements of bilingualism within the public service.
3.	The payment of an additional salary as a reward for the additional competence required from the civil servants who have to do business in both languages.
4.	The setting up, in each department, of a section concerned with the progress and coordination of the measures intended to ensure bilingualism.
5.	The setting up, location and structure of a federal institute where civil servants would study especially the problems relating to bilingualism and biculturalism.
6.	The use of bilingual forms, manuals and circulars in all departments and crown corporations.
7.	Bilingualism within our armed forces.
Of course the government reserves the right
to accept, amend or reject the recommendations made by the interdepartmental committee.
Moreover, we do not intend to impose that over-all program by force. We believe, on the contrary, that it would fail without full and wholehearted support from civil servants and their associations.
That is why the government intends to consult with these associations before taking each important step in that program. We want above all to avoid affecting acquired rights and creating new discriminatory conditions while trying to rectify the injustices that exist at the present time.
It must be added that many civil servants have already understood the new tasks which force themselves upon them and, in many cases, they have themselves taken the initiative by attending special classes, devoting part of their leisure time and their own money to that purpose. We are then convinced that civil servants will accept the government program concerning bilingualism, not reluctantly and as a concession but as an opportunity to improve their own culture and thence be able to serve all Canadians more effectively.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee appreciates the statement which the minister has just given to us. It was one of some length, and I do not say that critically at all. The subject matter deserves to be treated at some length. This is the first really definite statement on the administration of his department, with particular reference to the report of the Glassco commission. I appreciate the fact that the minister has dealt at some considerable length with the report of the Glassco commission. He dealt also with the matters of bilingualism and biculturalism, which is a very important matter. I am sure the minister and the committee will appreciate the fact I do not dwell on that at any length at all because I think we agree, in general, with what he has said. However, for a few brief moments I want to deal with his references to the Glassco commission.
I can appreciate the problems which are confronting the government, and particularly confronting the minister, because, as I understand it, the minister is charged primarily with the responsibility of developing this situation. I appreciate what he says about the chairman of the treasury board. It is true that constitutionally the Minister of Finance is the chairman of treasury board, or at least is responsible for its administration. I doubt whether that practice has been carried out to the letter for some years. I do not think I am betraying any state secrets when I say that during the time when I was minister of national revenue, in fact before the government changed in 1957, I was informed, when Mr. Abbott was minister of finance, that the minister of national revenue acted as chairman of treasury board, or was acting chairman of treasury board. During the time when my colleague Mr. Fleming was minister of finance, I very often, in fact usually, acted as chairman of treasury board; and when I became minister of finance I had another colleague take over the same responsibilities. Because it is absolutely impossible, of course, for a minister of finance to look after the details of matters which come before treasury board.
I think we are very fortunate in having had this report of the Glassco commission which points out the detailed administration which vests in treasury board today. With all respect to a most distinguished and able group of civil servants-no government could be better served-it is very difficult indeed for treasury board to deal adequately with these problems which confront them. I have been sitting in the public accounts committee during the last few days listening to discussion by hon. members about investigating tenders and other matters which come

Supply-Privy Council before treasury board. I have felt from listening to these hon. members that they did not realize that every week hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of these matters come before treasury board and have to be dealt with on the recommendations of the officials. It is impossible for the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue or for anyone-I understand that under the present government a colleague of the Minister of Finance acts as chairman most of the time- to deal with these problems. Therefore I appreciate the fact that the minister has dealt at some length today with his thinking with respect to the report of the Glassco commission.
I know very well that in the relatively short time which he has had at his disposal it is impossible for him to make definitive recommendations to the committee. I quite appreciate the fact that he will need some weeks, perhaps some months, longer to deal with the question. Perhaps I am pessimistic enough to think that he will have another three or four months in which to deal with these matters, and that when he brings his estimates before the committee of supply, which will have to be fairly early if he is going to deal with them, say in the early spring of next year, we will expect the minister to bring forward, as I am sure he is planning to do, positive recommendations or statements of policy as to how far he or the government proposes to go in implementing the Glassco commission report.
I know that the government of which I was a member was impressed with many of the recommendations in the report. We did not endorse them all, but I think there are matters there which are worthy of debate and should be considered very carefully before they are adopted. We did second to the privy council several civil servants, two of whom were particularly able; the deputy minister of a department who had had wide administrative experience and in whom I am sure every member of the House of Commons and member of this committee has complete confidence, and a Mr. McDonald, who had been a member of the treasury board, who co-operated with him. I am sure the minister is having the assistance of these senior civil servants, as well as undoubtedly many others in formulating his plans.
Without taking up too much time just now, because frankly one could talk about this matter for two hours and end up with the same situation-that there has not been time for the minister or the government to arrive at definite conclusions as to what they propose to do in this matter-may I just say that I think it is highly important that something should be done. I think the report is very


valuable. 1 hope and believe that the minister also feels there are many recommendations deserving of support which will result in economies in an area in which economies are very difficult to achieve; hence any avenue which leads to economies should be explored in every way.
I do not think I can usefully add anything more at this moment to what I have already said on the other question of bilingualism and biculturalism. This is a problem which has been with us for many years. I know the government is dealing or is intending to deal with it, and I am sure the committee and the House of Commons will support the government in every reasonable step they think necessary to develop the matter. So far as the Glassco commission is concerned I leave the report on the desk of the minister who is responsible for it, and look forward, as I said not later than the last of February or very early in March, to the recommendations which the minister will bring forward; otherwise it might be left on my desk, and I would rather have his recommendations to deal with at the moment than my own.

Mr. Chairman, a short while ago I met the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) and I told him that as far as I am concerned I would not delay the adoption of his estimates, because I was not supposed to speak. However, since the spokesman of our party is not in the house at this moment, I will therefore say a few words in his place.
I believe that we should congratulate the government for its goodwill shown in the two fields mentioned by the President of the Privy Council. He referred to the report, or reports of the Glassco commission. Although with some reservations, he has nevertheless proved that the government favours the implementation of certain parts of the report and a more detailed consideration of some others. It seems to be sincerely interested in the Glassco report.
The government ought to be commended in that connection. I believe our group would agree with me when I say that it is a step in the right direction, that of justice and equity.
The minister also referred to the Therrien minority report. There again, I feel that Mr. Therrien did well in submitting such a report even though he did not suggest any corrective measure. I have the impression that the government and the President of the Privy Council will do their utmost to find a solution to the problems set out by Mr. Therrien.
It is a well-known fact that the government intends to favour bilingualism, and I say that it deserves to be congratulated for the projects which the minister has announced in that respect.
It should be kept in mind that, according to the proverb or saying, the road to hell is paved with good intentions. Further steps are required and a definite stand should certainly be taken to cope with those problems.
I must admit that this problem is extremely complicated and that the Laurendeau-Dunton royal commission will not succeed in solving it. An answer will only be found with the good will of every individual, of parliament and, on a larger scale, of the Canadian people. It is only through understanding that we shall finally find a proper solution.

There is a great deal of talk about national unity, the union of our two nations. Indeed, several expressions are used in that respect. To prevent any ambiguity, we should speak of the good will which should exist between the various groups which form our country. However, we should recognize the fact that the two groups which founded Canada have certain rights and responsibilities of which immigrants should be aware before they come over here.
As far as culture is concerned, I do not admit that it must divide us; on the contrary, it must unite us and give us a better understanding of each other. Thus, through our various cultures rather than our languages, I am of the opinion that we should look for things we have in common, which would help us to agree instead of disagree.
I express the wish, since there is often talk of bilingualism, that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) will see to it that this commission will really give us an idea of the reasons why we find ourselves in such a situation today and let us know if there is a way out.
Before closing, I would like to add that my fellow citizens in Quebec with whom I am often in contact and to whom I offer applications to join the civil service, tell me: We do not want to go to Ottawa, we do not want to work for a federal department, we do not want to take a cut in salary in Ottawa when we can do better elsewhere.
Those are important problems and if we are aware of them, it will help us change an established situation of which we are conscious and about which even the royal commission will not give us much information.

I would like to speak about education, but in a much more limited way with regard to the rather serious problem that exists so far as the future of physicians in Canada is concerned. The education of physicians has become a very serious matter, much more serious than we realize, and in order to go into this subject I would like to preface it with three questions; (1) Are we producing enough physicians in Canada? (2) How does the quality of the physicians we produce compare with those produced in other countries? (3) What does the future hold.
The answer to the first question must be a categorical no. In the year 1901 Canada had one physician for every 972 persons. In the year 1951 there was one physician for 976

persons. Although our production of physicians from our own medical schools had increased during these years, it had not increased as rapidly as had the population of our country. Fortunately for us we were saved from a disastrous shortage of physicians during the past 10 years of rapid population growth by the large number of immigrant physicians who came to our country. The average output of our own 12 medical schools in Canada at the present time is about 850 new physicians a year. During some of the years since 1955 the immigrant physicians coming to our country have annually numbered over 600, thus increasing by approximately 75 per cent the number of physicians entering practice in Canada each year over what we produce ourselves. As a result of this, our physician population ratio has improved and in 1960 it was one to 879 population. It still is below that of 20 other countries in the world today, and far below the United States, which has one physician to 711 population.
Even if it were advantageous for Canadians to be looked after in significant part by physicians educated elsewhere, we cannot count on this source of supply to continue. Many of these immigrant physicians were the ones who were unhappy under some form of prepaid health insurance that existed in their own countries. As the years go by the number of malcontents becomes less, in part because physicians have been more inured to the new system, and in part because forms of prepaid health insurance in other countries have been improving as the difficulties in their early years of use have been smoothed out. Further, when Canada develops a form of government supported prepaid medical care itself, which most assuredly will happen, it will cease to be one of the few remaining centres of individual enterprise in the field of health.
Another factor which will make our supply of physicians still less adequate is the fact that when Canada does develop a form of government supported prepaid health insurance, there will be a significant increase in the demand for health services. In some other countries where this has been studied, the demand has increased by as much as 30 per cent. It is doubtful that the increase will be so great in Canada, because it seems likely that a larger proportion of our population is now receiving adequate medical care than in many other countries. However, there can be no doubt that there will be increased demand for physicians under any form of government supported health plan which is likely to come into effect in this country. Thus, at the moment when our demand for physician services will increase, we are likely to be 28902-5-364

Still another factor enters the situation. I shall not go into detail on this at the moment but will touch on it a little later. Medical education has been founded upon the fact that there are charity patients, and on these patients Canadian doctors have learned how to practise medicine. When health insurance is universal in Canada, charity patients will cease to exist. This will present a problem of the first magnitude in the training of physicians in this country. Under the circumstances, I hope you will agree with me that we are not educating a sufficient number of physicians.
The second question is: How does the quality of physicians produced in Canada compare with those produced in other countries? Teaching hospitals have been tremendously important in Canada's history. Apart from providing the medical student, the interne and the resident with patients over whom they could have certain responsibilities under supervision, they have been the locations in which clinical investigation has been centered. They have provided areas in which treatment methods could be evaluated under controlled circumstances. Their carefully selected physicians have been responsible for almost all the progress which has been made in medical care in this country. The physicians selected to serve on their staffs considered it to be an honour and the faculties of medicine had access to the services of these outstanding physicians for a part of each day for a tiny honorarium each year. Most of the patients in these units were charity patients from the community, referred in by the practising physician because such referral did not mean a loss of income. However, many others were the serious problem cases of the region requiring the excellent facilities and staffs provided. Truly the nerve centre of Canadian medicine has been the closed teaching units developed in our centres of medical education.
So medical education has progressed rapidly. That provided in Canada could compare favourably with that in any part of the world and as short a time as eight years ago Canadians had every reason to be proud of the physicians that were being produced in this country. However, since that time a whole series of events have entered the scene to make it difficult or impossible to maintain the standard which had been set previously. These I would like to enumerate.
First, forces have come into play which have tended to break down the strong union between the medical school and the teaching hospital. One of these forces has been a diminution in the number of charity patients

Supply-Privy Council and therefore a diminution in the interdependence of the two. As a result of the growth of voluntary prepaid medical plans large numbers of people are already covered for medical care. This is particularly true in the large centres of population wherein universities and medical schools are likely to be situated. Thus the number of charity patients to be referred to the teaching unit has diminished and in many schools in Canada a very real shortage of teaching patients is developing.
A second and more sudden influence has been the introduction of government supported hospitalization. In the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act made law on April 1, 1959, no mention was made of medical education. As a result, provincial hospital commissions have mostly taken the attitude that the additional costs of the teaching hospital, which previously had been supported by voluntary funds, were not a responsibility under the national hospital insurance agreement. Therefore, although every dollar required for the provision of routine care to the patient is provided in the main, no single penny is available for the added costs associated with medical education and with medical research. Further, the hospitals now being government supported are unable to continue their fund raising activities successfully. As a result, hospitals have not been able to continue to support medical education and medical research. The costs have been thrown back directly on the small and already strained budgets of the universities, and it is a fact that the universities have been subsidizing the national hospital insurance plan. As a result of these two influences the strong union between the teaching hospital and the medical school is rapidly breaking down in our country and producing a serious problem in medical education.
This has not been true in other countries which have embraced government support of health care. In the United Kingdom the teaching hospital is the recognized centre of the hospital region. It is accepted that its costs will be from 25 per cent to 30 per cent higher per patient-day than those of any other hospital in the region. Its facilities are greater, its staff is larger and its patient clientele is assured because it is the only hospital in the district that can look after problem cases. In Sweden, despite a prepaid system outside the hospital, the same arrangements prevail inside the hospital as occur in the United Kingdom and thus the patients and the facilities to ensure the training of physicians are assured. A second influence which increasingly enters the scene is represented by the rapidly spiralling costs of medical education. Standards are being set in other countries

which our universities are desperately trying to meet without adequate sources of funds.
I have explained how in the United Kingdom the additional costs of clinical teaching are considered part and parcel of the health care plan. In the United States the solution was found in quite a different way. It was painfully obvious that medical education needed more financial support than it was receiving from the education budget. There were problems associated with federal sources of funds being granted to state supported medical schools for educational purposes. Accordingly the federal government of the United States has undertaken to support medical schools indirectly by huge increases in the grants available for medical research, virtually all of which is done in medical schools. The speed and extent of the explosion of these funds can best be illustrated by outlining the budgets for government support of medical research in the U.S.A. in the past few years. For several years, up to and including 1959, there was approximately $250 million available for support of medical research in the United States. Most of this was going to the 87 medical schools in that country. In the year 1960 this was increased from $250 million to $425 million; in 1961 it was increased to $650 million; in 1962 it was increased to $890 million, and in 1963 it is no less than $1,100 million.
After removing a significant amount of these funds to pay for the federally operated medical research laboratories in Bethesda, Maryland, and other centres, there still remains an enormous amount of money to be divided among the 87 medical schools in that country. During this year, if the money were averaged it would amount to approximately $10 million per medical school. In Canada the total sum of money from government sources available for the support of medical research is about $12 million and would provide each of our 12 medical schools, if it were evenly divided among them, with something less than $1 million per year. Thus the 12 universities in Canada which have undertaken the responsibility or the education of physicians have been desperately trying to find the funds to put their medical schools in a position in which they can compete with other medical schools on this continent. The medical schools are taking an embarrassingly large percentage of the total university budget for a very small percentage of the total students. In the University of British Columbia 9.5 per cent of the budget goes to the support of 1.5 per cent of the students who are in the medical school. Despite the heroic efforts that have been made by universities

to keep pace with what is going on in medical education in other countries, they are fighting a losing battle.
Over this long open border between the United States and Canada there is great freedom of interchange of medical scientists. Over 5,000 Canadian educated physicians are now living within that country. Most of these physicians have gone there to practise, but in recent years a much more serious trend has developed. Partly because we cannot compete either in salary scales or in working conditions, we are tending to lose more of our most able medical educators to that country. More important perhaps is the fact that with the facilities and staff that can be obtained under these very generous research grants, there are research potentials in the United States which are not available in our country. Thus the very core of our system of medical education and medical research is in danger of being lost to another country.
In recent months a new factor has entered the situation. Legislation has been enacted in the United States which provides federal sources of funds for the building of teaching facilities for medical schools in that country. Thus teaching hospitals and buildings in which the basic medical sciences can be taught will now be very largely supported from the federal government in addition to the support for the operation of these schools.
There is one other point concerning unfortunate factors which have come into being in recent years which must be mentioned. The number of individuals applying to medical school in this country fell steadily from the post-war peak to the year 1958. During the years 1955 to 1958, in particular, we were terribly concerned about our ability to fill even our inadequate number of places with reasonable students. Since 1958 there has been an increase in the number applying for medicine. However, we do not believe that this increase is the result of any change in forces that are being brought to bear on the situation. Rather it is because the post-war baby boom has reached the stage of entry to medical school, and we are simply deriving our applicants to medical school from a temporarily larger group of people who are attending university.
There is obviously more than one reason for this diminution of people attending medical schools. Fifty years ago a very high percentage of all the young people who entered university found their way into medical schools. Apart from law and the church, there were few other attractive careers available to them. Now a very small percentage of the total number of students who enter universities come to medical school. This factor has been in operation in every country in the past half century, but in our country still another factor has come into operation in recent years. Some years ago in an attempt to increase the number of individuals attracted into the physical sciences, such as chemistry and physics, the government, through the national research council, created a subsidization program. This program provides that once a good student has obtained his bachelor's degree in the physical sciences, he is supported in the amount of approximately $2,200 for whatever number of years is required to obtain his Ph.D. degree.
The future members of the health sciences of this country, the physicians and the dentists must be selected from capable young students who have shown an interest in the general field of science. However, let us compare the financial problems facing the student who wishes to enter the field of medicine with the student who wishes to enter the field of science. In most schools in Canada it is at the end of the third year of university that he must make this decision. If the student decides in favour of physics or chemistry, he has one more year in which to pay his fees at the university until he receives his baccalaureate degree. Thereafter, if he is a good student, he will receive the government subsidization program for the three or four years necessary to obtain his Ph.D. and will then be able to step into a well paid position. In contrast, the student wishing to enter medicine must pay four years of the highest fees which the university charges for the remainder of his undergraduate medical education, with no subsidization program available to help him. He must then take a minimum of one year's interneship, which would barely provide him with enough remuneration on which to subsist. If he wishes to proceed to specialty training, he will require four more years of a bare subsistence income before he can begin to go further into debt by setting up his office and awaiting the arrival of his first paying patient.
Is there any wonder that the number of individuals applying to enter medicine in Canada has diminished in recent years, and is there any wonder that this diminution in numbers is particularly notable among the brighter students who are assured of the subsidization program if they go into other areas? I think it must be made very clear that, if a subsidization program is instituted for one part of the field of science to the

Supply-Privy Council exclusion of the remainder of that field, it will cause an entirely artificial emphasis on those areas which are being subsidized. I fear that, unless we do something to more nearly equalize the financial problems of higher education in these various groups, we may, 25 years from now, pay very heavily in a reduced level of medical care in our country.
To summarize our second question, after achieving an extremely high level of medical education in our country, three apparently unrelated forces have come into being in recent years which have reduced that level. These are:
1.	Lack of recognition that teaching hospitals must receive a greater degree of support than usual general hospitals.
2.	Rapid increase in support of medical education in other countries.
3.	Subsidization of other science students in Canada.
The acuteness of the present situation can perhaps be best illustrated by events which have taken place within the past year. In the United States and Canada there is an accreditation panel for medical schools. Approximately every eight years every medical school on this continent is visited by a team of medical educators. The school is studied intensely over a period of several days. Thereafter a report is written describing the school and a recommendation goes to the association of American medical colleges as to whether this school should or should not continue to be accredited. Failure to obtain accreditation means a school really must close its doors. Because of the difference in the degree of financial support of medical schools in the United States and Canada a difficult task faces the evaluators. It is just not possible to apply to Canadian schools the same high standards as are being applied to American schools. Perhaps this is best summarized in the words of Dean Chester Stewart of Dalhousie University, in his report to the Canadian universities foundation earlier this year at the end of his term of office as president of the association of Canadian medical colleges. Dr. Stewart stated:
It is probably well known to most university teachers that medical education in Canada has made immense forward strides. Our medical schools have become the equal of any in the world and have made outstanding contributions to the development of medical education and research. Perhaps few are aware, however, of the rapidly widening gap between progress in medical education in the United States and Canada. We would ask the Canadian universities foundation to consider the implications of what has been frankly called "the double standard of medical education on this continent", a comment by a senior member of the accrediting bodies. It would be little short of tragic if some of our Canadian medical schools were to lose their status as fully

accredited institutions just at a time when there is a growing pressure for the expansion of medical school facilities in order to meet the physician requirements of this country.
I am not by nature a pessimist and I do not enjoy the role of being a prophet of doom and gloom. However, I feel strongly that if we, in our country, fail to keep pace with other countries in the support of educational opportunities in the field of medicine, we will pay a heavy price in the years ahead in the quality of medical care available to us. Immediately we will pay the price of losing our most able teachers and investigators to those parts of the world where the necessary support is available to them.
Now the final question is: What does the future hold? I think this can be answered briefly. If Canadians are to receive adequate health care in future the 12 universities that have taken on the responsibility for the education of physicians must have more assistance. I think it is appropriate that this assistance come from federal sources of funds. A medical school is much more than a local asset. Physicians travel widely both in their post-graduate training and in their subsequent locations of practice. The increased sources of funds provided to medical schools must be for three purposes:
1.	There must be a very significant increase in the support of the day to day cost of medical schools. A very significant proportion of this could be taken care of by including the cost of clinical medical education in the Diagnostic Services and Hospital Insurance Act. Without increasing significantly the tremendous sums of money which are now going to the support of hospitalization, the problems of the medical schools in Canada could be sharply reduced.
2.	Assistance must be provided for the development of buildings both for teaching and for research. Such assistance was recommended by Dr. Ray Farquharson's special committee two years ago. Although accepted in principle, no action has been taken by government. We do not have a single university owned and operated hospital in the twelve medical schools of our country. We are dependant upon the use of general hospitals in the communities in which the medical school is located. While this has worked well in the past, the interest of these general hospitals is increasingly in conflict vuth the interests of medical education, as I have tried to point out.
3.	We need support and subsidization for students entering into the health science field. At the present time 84 per cent of all medical students depend largely on their parents' funds to put them through school. Approximately 20 per cent of graduate students in the fields of science depend to any

degree on parental assistance. As long as this situation exists, a proper share of the bright young minds of Canada will not be directed towards a medical career and in future the health of our country will suffer.
