Now, I would suggest to the premier of Quebec, who sat for a long time in this house, who occupied a ministerial position, and who certainly knows the weaknesses of the federal civil service, in so far as French speaking Canadians are concerned, that he would certainly be in a position to have a special budget voted in order to create a university department to prepare French Canadian civil servants to come to Ottawa to occupy the place that belongs to them.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to resort to an article which was published in Le Devoir on August 19 last, to make the next few remarks. The writer of the article was Mr. Jean-Pierre Fournier. Here is what he had to say:
Even though the administration school which the federal government intends to establish is not

useless, it could not be the key to bilingualism in the public service.
(1) On the one hand, the essential point is not to enable classified civil servants to acquire a fluent knowledge of both languages, but to ensure to French Canada its just representation at all levels of the civil service, based on the proportion of the French Canadian population.
Mr. Chairman, the fact of the matter is that in Ottawa, we have a problem with translators and interpreters; I take this opportunity to point out to the minister that the only way to find a sufficient number of them is to increase their salary. I suggest they be offered a more attractive remuneration, as they are hard to find. I am told they are few and far between in Canada, and that the best means to attract them to Ottawa is to offer them a higher salary.
I also suggest to the minister that civil servants in categories 1 and 2, be also granted an increase. I believe those are the only categories which have been overlooked, when the salaries of the federal civil servants were revised.
Mr. Chairman, quite recently, on October 18 last, Le Devoir published an article with the following title.
Ottawa-eight civil servants denounce the fate of Quebec university graduates.
The article quoted a letter signed by eight federal civil servants. I would like the minister to check the facts pointed out by the newspaper. Could the minister tell us whether he has personally looked into the matter?
Mr. Chairman, the minister told us about forthcoming reforms. I put on the order paper a question asking how many bilingual employees worked in the Prime Minister's office. I must tell you frankly that I was disappointed when I read the answer given me. In fact, I noticed that there is great difference in the number of French speaking, and English speaking employees in the Prime Minister's office. And I ask the minister to remedy that situation so that the government itself and, therefore, the Prime Minister, will set an example to create a favourable climate and, indirectly, attract more French speaking Canadians to take their place in Ottawa.
Mr. Chairman, before closing, I ask the minister if it might not be time to study the possibility of setting up a research office for all the members of the house so that they may have all the information they need to prepare their speeches and the questions they put on the order paper or ask in the house. I know that such a body exists in other countries and I see no reason why experts should not be available to inform the members, thus helping them to make a better contribution to the debates of the house, and at the same time being of service to their country.

Mr. Chairman, I wish the minister well. The work had already been started; he showed his good faith by telling us that he wants to follow it up by carrying out the recommendations contained in the Glassco report and those in the Therrien minority report. Therefore, I wish him well, and next year, when his estimates are introduced, we shall ask him to report the progress made.

I should like to take up a few minutes of the time of this committee, while we are discussing the estimates of the privy council, to make a proposal. First, I should like to say I am very much in accord with the suggestions made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and by the hon. member for Queens with regard to education. On previous occasions I have made contributions to debate in which the same ideas were promulgated.
In making the proposal I have in mind, let me say at the outset that it is not put forward by my party; it is being made by myself, though I would hope my party would not oppose it. I trust, also, that this proposal would not have any tinge of partisanship attached to it. In fact, I am sure it could not succeed if it carried any such stigma. Certainly, none is intended on my part and I would hope, if the proposal were accepted, that none would be allowed to creep in. Further, may I say that the proposal is not mine. It is the brainchild of a young Saskatchewan man who believes it would be a popular and attractive way of celebrating our centenary year in 1967.
I am sure we all feel too much could not be done to emphasize the importance of our 100th birthday. But nothing seems to have been planned for one most important group-a group which is just ready to step on to the stage of life and a group which is sometimes unjustly maligned-the teenagers. It is to this group that my suggestion is directed. Baldly stated, it is that a youth parliament be held in Ottawa in the summer of 1967. Many details would have to be worked out before such a parliament could be held. We would have to decide how many delegates there should be, how they should be selected, just when and where the parliament would be held, and a great many other similar questions. Assistance could, perhaps, be given by some of our national service groups. If these groups could be persuaded to give their support it would, no doubt, mean a great deal to any such scheme.
I have here an article from the Daily Gleaner of Fredericton which sets down in some detail the various things which could be done in connection with this proposal, and
Supply-Privy Council some of the difficulties which might arise. If I might have the approval of the house I would like to have this article incorporated in the report of my remarks as they will appear in Hansard. I do not think I will read it, because I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by elaborating this proposal in detail.
This scheme is, perhaps, most worth while because it might show us and the people of this country the characteristic which is so strong in this group-the forward-looking idealism which in the past has so often given us an impetus for making reforms. There is already a basis for a scheme such as I have suggested, since youth parliaments are in operation now in some areas, notably in my own province of Saskatchewan. I sincerely believe that this plan is worthy of serious consideration and I therefore respectfully suggest to the Prime Minister that an appointed committee consisting of two government supporters, two from the official opposition, two from the New Democratic party, one from Ralliement Creditistes and one from the Social Credit party be convened to consider it further, and to bring in recommendations to this parliament relative to it.

I rise briefly to support the pleas made by previous members who have spoken urging the government to give immediate and serious consideration tp the needs of universities which require plant and equipment, and to the question of scholarships and loans for students.
I have been asked by graduates and students of the universities of British Columbia, Victoria and Notre Dame who are resident in my constituency to remind the government of the election pledge to provide 10,000 scholarships valued at $1,000 each. This is a pledge which was taken seriously by young people throughout the country, and by many other Canadians who are expecting the government to keep that promise. In fact, some of these young students planned their future activities in the hope of winning one of these scholarships, but I must say that what has happened so far has not justified their confidence in the promises made by government spokesmen during the election campaign.
However, in my opinion even these scholarships will not by any means meet the rapidly growing need for assistance to universities and to students. I presume that assistance to students will be of two types. First, there will be scholarships for those who are able to win scholarships and demonstrate their particular skill and ability to do so. Then I believe there should be a system of loans. I am not one who believes

Supply-Privy Council that you should hand out something for nothing to young people. I believe that you value what you earn. In my view we should establish a sound system of loans available to students who have the ability to go through university and to apply that ability to university studies, advanced studies and so on.
I might say that I discussed this problem recently with a person who is very interested in education. We were considering the problem in relation to the circumstances of the country, the financial ability of the federal and provincial governments to meet these needs and the fact that this should be done on some sound basis, not just on the basis of handing out money wholesale to anybody who says he wants to attend university. This gentleman asked me to bring this point to the attention of the minister. I thought it was a rather novel suggestion. He suggested that consideration should be given to loans to students who could take advantage of such loans-there would have to be some winnowing out-and who would graduate, and as a result greatly improve their earning ability. He went on to suggest that these loans could be repaid on the basis of the government establishing an education tax of 1, 2 or 3 per cent of their income, whatever might be necessary, over a period of years in their earning life so that repayment would not be a heavy burden on them in their first earning years, but would be on a sound basis. I do not know whether consideration has been given to that sort of scheme but I suggest that it merits consideration, as well as other schemes that will make it possible for young, capable persons to obtain loans from the federal or provincial governments as the result of federal-provincial co-operation. These could be repaid in such a way that they would not constitute a great strain on them in their early earning years. With these few remarks I resume my seat.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make about the estimates of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamon-tagne).
In fact, I must tell you that before knowing him as the President of the Privy Council, I knew him most of all as an orthodox economist. It is only since becoming a member of this house and President of the Privy Council that he has directed his activity to other fields, for instance to the reports submitted by the various commissions or federal-provincial relations which, I think, come first among his functions.
I feel, however, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was well advised to change his
[Mr. Herridge.l
field of activity because in this one he can show greater efficiency than in the other.
I see that the President of the Privy Council does not seem to appreciate my qualifying his talent in economics as conventional, but it seems to me that he follows mainly the antiquated methods and doctrines of the 19th century, if not of the 18th, as far as political economy is concerned.
I have some remarks to make and I think that the President of the Privy Council is well disposed to receive fruitfully these remarks and try to find solutions to the few problems I would like to point out today.
First of all, I would like to raise a problem which I consider important. I listened last Sunday to the press conference given by the Quebec premier, Mr. Jean Lesage, during the television program on public affairs or political events of the day. I do not know whether the President of the Privy Council had the opportunity to listen to that program. He nods; he will then understand my remarks all the better. I found during the program that the premier of Quebec showed a really pitiful attitude and talked in a soppy tone. In short, he looked depressed and in low spirits after returning almost empty-handed from the federal-provincial conference.
Being aware of the legendary courage of the premier of Quebec, I thought he would soon abandon that pitiful and soppy attitude, that the reaction would set in before long and that he would deliver new ultimatums, taking a really resolute stand, in order to get what the province of Quebec claims, faced with its priority needs.
I suggest that the President of the Privy Council should not wait for that reaction to set in but that he should undertake an open-minded examination of Quebec's requests and problems and, as the hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Caouette) would say, to consider in a more broadminded spirit the problems which interest both the provincial and federal governments and to accede to Quebec's legitimate requests.
If the President of the Privy Council looked at that program he must have noticed that the Quebec premier looked depressed and beaten. I hope he will react and show more firmness than he did in the past because when he starts changing the word "demand" for "request" or "require" his most simple requests remain unsatisfied. It is inferred that in order to obtain something from the federal government, a firmer stand must still be taken.
I ask the President of the Privy Council who is, I believe, a friend of the Quebec premier and who understands, not only the requests of that premier, but also those of

all the people in Quebec, to help find a solution to those problems by meeting the priority requirements of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that the province of Quebec, especially after the reaction felt among the public following Ottawa's refusal to comply with its requests, will tolerate much longer to be treated as it was at the last federal-provincial conference. The general disappointment which was noted among the people is an indication that the province of Quebec will no longer tolerate its requests being turned down.
Another point which, in my opinion, comes under the President of the Privy Council, and for which he should make claims and use pressure, is the statement made yesterday or the day before by the mayor of Ottawa to the effect that Ottawa is and will remain an unilingual city.
As we are in the city of Ottawa, I feel we have the right to speak French in this city. People are talking of bilingualism, but this should not stop there, it must become a reality, without it being necessary to ask permission from the Ontario government. Considering the importance of the city of Ottawa in the country, since it is the capital and the seat of central government, where French speaking as well as English speaking members of parliament sit, we must see to it that everyone feels at home here and is welcomed by persons having a sense of hospitality.
When we talk about bilingualism, we do not seek to take away anything from other people; we merely want for everybody the right to speak his own language. Now, in the federal capital, we would not like to be deprived of this right.
I would describe the mayor of Ottawa as a female tyrant.
It is true.

I may say that I was very happy to see that the English speaking newspapers condemned her backward attitude. It obviously indicates that the English speaking press understands the situation and, more rightly so, the nation's capital ought to proclaim itself a completely bilingual city, since citizens representing ridings all over the country live there. I shall add that when the mayor of Ottawa comes in the province of Quebec, she is welcome, she may speak her own language, she is understood in her own language, because, in the province of Quebec, we are happy to receive her in a bilingual fashion. Let her do the same thing in the country's capital.
I recognize she may have some inhibitions which lead her to vent her spleen occasionally. In my opinion, she could have vented

Supply-Privy Council her ill-humour on another matter. There is precisely an opera aria which is entitled "La donna e mobile" or "Like a Feather in the Air". I believe that on the subject of bilingualism, the mayor of Ottawa could be more serious and stop going around "like a feather in the air", as is said in that famous opera by Verdi.
Mr. Chairman, I would now like to touch on a point which gave rise to several remarks in the Canadian press recently, that is, the presence of the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines at the meeting of the parliamentary committee on railways, air lines and shipping. In my opinion, this is in order, since the subject concerns the question of relations between the two great nations which form this country. In that respect, I would like to make a correction. There is no question of blaming the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines for his attitude towards bilingualism in the country. On the contrary, I believe it is in Trans-Canada Air Lines, among all the crown corporations, that bilingualism is the most respected.
The ratio maintained at T.C.A., that is 28 per cent of the employees being French Canadian or bilingual, would seem acceptable to me. Mr. McGregor stated the other day a commendable fact when he said that for the last year, no employee who has to come in contact with the public has been hired unless he was bilingual, that is able to be understood by the two great nations living in this country. I have no fear in saying that we must encourage Mr. McGregor and admit that he possesses a real sense of bilingualism. Indeed, within his corporation, nothing suits him better than to meet his obligation in that field.
But he is blameworthy on another point, that is for his adamant attitude in hiding from Canadians facts which they have the right to know. In view of the unkind remarks by the president of T.C.A. for the Sud-Avia-tion Corporation and the Caravelle aircraft, people are justified to ask why they refuse to build that aircraft in Montreal, thus enabling Montreal workers to earn a livelihood when there is unemployment.
In fact, the experts' report seemed to have been brushed aside. We do not object if workers are employed at the general maintenance base in Winnipeg, if Winnipeg workers earn a livelihood, but we wonder why a report by experts is brushed aside when a French aircraft is involved, when Montreal is concerned. We are given no reason, no argument. They refuse to produce the report and they are unkind and even unscrupulous towards the Sud-Aviation Corporation.
Montreal workers are not given satisfaction and that is what the people of the

Supply-Privy Council province of Quebec cannot tolerate. How come the public is not allowed to examine the report? Security is given as a pretext while nowadays, all over the world, in South America as well as in Europe, people never cease praising the qualities of that aircraft in terms of security and they even go as far as saying it is the safest aircraft in the world at the present time. We are given no reason and we wonder whether it is not a matter of favouring the United States.
That is the opinion among the people of Quebec and it is derived from the evidence given by Mr. McGregor concerning the purchase of new airplanes.

Mr. Chairman, I may appear at this stage to filibuster my own estimates, but I promised some weeks ago to make a statement on centennial agencies and centennial projects and programs. I believe this kind of statement will be useful at this stage, not only to members of the house and members of this committee but also to the population in general. I want first to deal with the centennial agencies. It may appear to the casual observer from this point of view that there is a surfeit of organizations, agencies and structures throughout Canada for planning the centennial. This may be a legitimate complaint at the moment, but I believe that once programs begin to emerge involving the three levels of government and private organizations in every part of the country, these agencies will each find their role and serve their purpose as they are meant to.
In the private sector, the Canadian centenary council has been established "to stimulate interest and to educate the Canadian public for appropriate observances of the anniversary of confederation in 1967 by encouraging, undertaking and assisting centenary projects of a lasting and beneficial nature to the community". I have quoted from their constitution. This Canadian centenary council is a purely private and voluntary body which is designed to work in close co-operation with private organizations while maintaining close liaison with government agencies. I am convinced that the council will play a most useful role in the preparation of the centennial celebrations, as I said in a recent letter to its president, Dr. Norman MacKenzie. I would like to quote briefly from that letter:
-the Prime Minister and all members of the government are in full agreement about the importance of thought and action directed toward the centenary by individual citizens and by their many private organizations...
For maximum effect these efforts of Canadian citizens and Canadian organizations must have a focal point, a centre for clearance, for planning and for the exchange of views and experience. Outside the national centennial administration, which is the federal agency established by law for the purpose of planning the centennial with a national approach, the Canadian centenary council represents the only national voluntary organization whose sole purpose and object is to further centennial planning...
We have been pleased to note not only the existence of the Canadian centenary council, and its accomplishments during the past few years, but also its record of working effectively and harmoniously with the organizations established for 28902-5-3654

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I want to finish quoting from the letter to the president of the Canadian centenary council:
The federal government invites the Canadian centenary council to continue to work closely with the national centennial administration.
In the private sector all across the country voluntary associations, agencies and corporations are developing centennial programs. It is not the size of the project that counts. Some of them will be small by force of circumstances, but it is the total and the quality that count. I am informed that many of these voluntary programs, large and small, are already in operation.
In the public sector, a great number of municipalities have already set up local centennial committees and we hope that every municipality in Canada will have its own local committee in the near future. All provinces have designated a minister to be responsible for the centennial celebrations and most of them have set up their own provincial agencies. At the federal level, the government has constituted a cabinet committee on the 1967 program and an interdepartmental committee of officials which will coordinate all the activities of the different federal departments and agencies directly or indirectly related to the centennial celebrations.
The national centennial administration is the central federal agency charged with originating, developing and implementing projects and programs as approved by the governor in council. It has a specific responsibility for centennial projects which it will undertake itself within its own terms of reference, but it is also the agency of the federal government charged with the responsibility of implementing the federal program of grants for local centennial projects in collaboration with the provinces. Finally, it will play an important part in advising other federal departments and agencies on centennial projects conceived and developed directly by these

Supply-Privy Council departments. The national centennial administration is a crown corporation with a commissioner, a deputy commissioner and eight directors who were appointed in January, 1963. Since May of this year, the administration has been busy recruiting government personnel for the tremendous task ahead and developing these projects and programs.
Finally, there are two liaison agencies. The national committee on the centennial is responsible for liaison at government level. It is composed of two federal ministers and ten provincial ministers responsible for the centennial celebrations and their advisers. In other words, this national committee is a federal-provincial conference on the centennial. The national committee met in October of this year for the first time since 1961 and will meet again in the middle of December.
The national conference on the centennial is an over-all advisory and liaison agency which consists of 20 representatives, whose nominations were proposed by the provincial governments themselves, and of 40 members at large representing the different segments of the Canadian population. In addition, representatives from the Canadian centenary council and from youth movements are invited as observers. The national centennial administration provides its secretariat and its staff.
The national conference met for the first time in the middle of October this year in Ottawa. This meeting was, of course, of a preliminary nature. The general aspects of federal-provincial programs were reviewed and other centennial projects were also discussed. A steering committee was set up to act in an executive capacity. This committee met in November to prepare the next meeting of the conference which will be held in Ottawa next week.
This administrative set-up, with its various agencies, may seem to be unduly complicated and cumbersome. I believe, however, it reflects the character of our country with its federal structure and its sparse population distributed over a wide territory. I can assure hon. members also that everything will be done to avoid duplication and overlapping between these various agencies.
I should like now to report briefly on the centennial projects and programs which are under consideration at the present time. This report will be limited to those projects and programs which are directly connected with the federal government. They can be divided into two categories, capital works programs and other projects. The federal government will participate in financing or initiate three different capital works programs.
First, the federal government is offering assistance to local or regional capital works
[Mr. Lamontagne.l
projects. Federal grants are distributed through the national centennial administration and paid out of the national centennial fund. They are subject to varying conditions. First, an application for a federal grant, if it is for a local centennial project, must be made to the province. Second, the province must approve of the project and must assure the national centennial administration that two thirds of the cost will be met jointly by the province and the initiating agency. Third, the national centennial administration will pay up to one third of the estimated cost of approved projects, the grant being made to the province. Fourth, a project which is eligible for other forms of federal aid will also be eligible for a centennial grant, provided that the aggregate federal contribution does not exceed 50 per cent of the cost. Fifth, the total amount available under this program will be one dollar per capita of the province based on the population on June 1, 1963. Sixth, the projects must have a reasonable prospect of being completed by the time of the centennial observance. Seventh, anticipated revenue from the project will be taken into consideration in determining the amount of federal contribution.
A project must be of a lasting nature and might include, for example, acquisition and construction of buildings, parks and other capital works; the acquisition of buildings of historic or architectural merit; the restoration of buildings of historic or architectural merit; the writing and publishing of books; the composition of musical works, and the creation and completion of painting, sculpture and other works of art. However, it does not include any part of pageants or celebrations or administrative expenses of local committees.
This program will be implemented within the framework of specific federal-provincial agreements. The terms and conditions of these agreements have already been discussed in detail with all the provinces. Copies of the proposed agreements have been sent to the provincial governments several weeks ago. Four provinces have signed this agreement and others are expected to do so before the end of this year.
Thus, there will be no direct federal assistance to local or regional centennial projects of the capital works type. All requests for aid concerning such projects must be sent to provincial governments or to their centennial agencies rather than to the federal government or the national centennial administration.
The second program involving federal participation concerns provincial capital works projects. The federal government has agreed to pay 50 per cent of the cost of two buildings which will commemorate the two conferences held in Charlottetown and Quebec city in

1864. It is anticipated that early in May 1964, the Fathers of Confederation Memorial Building, Charlottetown, which is jointly financed by the federal government and by the ten provincial governments, will be completed and ready for use. This building will play a very important part next year in the special observances of the centennial of the 1864 confederation conference.
Another building for the performing arts will be erected in Quebec city to commemorate the Quebec conference. Construction work will begin next year. A special program of celebrations to commemorate those two historic conferences will be announced shortly.
Finally, the federal government will undertake a special building program in the capital district which will help to improve the cultural life and institutions, not only in the area but in the whole country. This program will include the national library and archives building, the national museum building, the redevelopment of confederation square, including possibly a convention centre and auditorium, and the restoration of the Thompson mill at Victoria island. Finally, the establishment of a national centre for the performing arts is under active consideration by the government.
The federal government is also developing another kind of program designed to prepare for, to celebrate or to commemorate the centennial. The acquisition and construction of buildings, parks and other permanent capital works will be excluded from this program. Eligible projects will be partly or wholly financed by the federal government and will have to be of a national or interprovincial character.
In order to celebrate the centennial, we must prepare for it. This means that Canadians, especially young people, must improve their knowledge of Canada and her history. We hope that Canadian teachers, especially in the field of history, will intensify their efforts in this respect. Beginning early next year, we intend to work in close co-operation with Canadian newspapers and magazines, as well as with our broadcasting networks and film producers to initiate special projects with these organizations if necessary in order to create greater interest in the centennial and its celebrations. We will also begin in 1964 to participate financially in an expanded youth travel and exchange program in collaboration with existing private organizations. We hope also Canadians, instead of criticizing what is done or not done in preparation for the centennial, will continue to send suggestions and proposals to the national centennial administration in Ottawa or to the Canadian centenary council or to the appropriate provincial authorities.

The preparation for the ceremonial program or the so-called birthday party has begun. Such projects as the confederation caravans, floating exhibits and a military searchlight tattoo are under consideration. Other projects for the centennial celebration are also being considered, such as a special travel program with particular emphasis on young Canadians, a series of international events to take place in Canada in 1967, an international and a national festival for the performing arts which would tour the main cities of our country.
In addition, other projects which would not only contribute to the celebration of the centennial but would also have a lasting value in commemorating the Canadian confederation are under study. They include such projects as a series of films on Canadian history, including a colour film on ethnic groups, the collection of basic documents on Indian history and culture to serve as source material, a centennial volume covering the Canadian centenary to be used by the dominion bureau of statistics, special editions of the Canada Year Book and the Canada Handbook, a definitive edition of the debates of the House of Commons from 1867 to 1874, a new edition of Canadian ministries since confederation, a biographical dictionary of all members and Senators since 1867, the papers of Canadian prime ministers commencing with Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, a bibliography of Cana-diana between 1867 and 1900, a series of lectures by distinguished personalities from abroad under the auspices of the national gallery, a possible new general issue of stamps for 1967 incorporating a centennial symbol, the establishment of a national symphony orchestra and of two national theatre groups, the sponsorship of national amateur festivals. Other suggestions are under review; a special coinage issue and medallions for school children, the commissioning of works of art, a Canadian anthology recommended by the Canadian authors association, a proposed youth parliament, as mentioned this afternoon, representative of all the constituencies of Canada to meet in the House of Commons. Finally, the Department of External Affairs is also considering special programs which would come under its direct responsibility.
We must try to make the centennial available to the maximum number of Canadians throughout the whole of Canada. This is why we are featuring exchanges and portable exhibits and encouraging Canadians to travel at home. We propose to do our best within the bounds of the sensible and practical to bring the centennial to the people of Canada.



Supply-Privy Council
Those are some of the projects which have been decided upon or are presently under active consideration. Some of these projects will be changed and reshaped or even replaced by others as the order of priorities is reassessed. Undoubtedly, other worth-while projects will be added to this list as our discussions and our work progress. I will be pleased to report to the house on projects and programs related to the centennial from time to time as decisions are reached.
This short report clearly indicates how the government intends to prepare and to celebrate the Canadian confederation centennial. We wish this great historical event to serve the purpose of proving as well as enhancing the Canadian people's cultural life.
Canada has made remarkable progress during the last century from the economic and even from the social standpoint. Previously to 1867, our country was made up of economically stagnating regions. Today, we are one of the wealthiest nations in the world. However, progress in our cultural life has not matched our economic and social progress.
Such a lack of balance brings to our mind the thought expressed by the French philosopher, Henri Bergson, as regards the whole modern world. Here is what he said:
Nature, in giving us an essentially active mind, had thus intended for us a certain development. But machines running on fuel, coal and white coal, and converting into motion potential energies accumulated for millions of years, have finally given to our system such tremendous expansion and power, which is so disproportionate to its size and strength, that surely nothing of the sort had been anticipated in the planned structure of our species.. .Now, in this inordinately expanded body, the soul remains what it was, too small now to fill it, too weak to direct it. Hence, the vacuum between body and soul. Hence, the formidable social, political and international problems which are so many indications of that vacuum and give rise, in order to fill it, to so many disorderly and inefficient efforts.. .The enlarged body calls for a greater soul.
Since 1867, our country has expanded physically and materially at an increasing rate. It now seems to be calling for a greater soul. It will achieve this only if it intensifies its cultural life, feeding its two main cultural streams and getting them to meet more often.
That is the major purpose the government of Canada would like to achieve for the centennial celebrations in close co-operation with the provincial governments, the municipalities, the leaders in the private sector and the greatest possible number of citizens.
If we succeed in giving to several of our cities suitable art centres, if we succeed in making of the Ottawa-Hull area a national centre where our two main cultures will be able to express themselves and to meet with the best they have to offer, if we succeed in
[Mr. Lamontagne.l
creating at least two national theatre groups, an orchestra, a ballet company, encouraging our artists to a greater extent, giving our young people the opportunity to meet and know their country better, if we succeed in knowing our history and background better thanks to the work of our researchers, we will be able to celebrate the centennial with a light heart, because we will have taken advantage together of this unique opportunity to give a new impulsion, a new start to our cultural life, to give a greater soul to our country.
There is little time left to prepare the celebration of the centennial of confederation but it is not too late, fortunately, if all men of good will agree to co-operate and work hard. The present government itself has not lost time and is now ready to carry out the various projects.
The national centennial administration is well established and will soon be able to operate fully. The national ministers' committee has been revived recently; the national conference has been established and will soon be divided into special committees. Those two agencies will meet again next week in Ottawa.
It remains, however, that the federal government cannot do everything by itself. The provinces, the municipalities and the leaders in the private sector will also have an important role to play.
In the last analysis, the success of the centennial celebrations will depend on the Canadians in general, on the interest they will take in them and on their active participation. We must therefore all work together so that 1967 will become a new start towards our destiny.

The Depuiy Chairman: The hon. member for Kindersley.
Hear, hear.

I appreciate that applause, especially since I rise to correct a mistake made in the course of my address earlier this afternoon. It had been my intention, when I spoke then, to ask for the inclusion in the report of my remarks of an article which appeared in the Daily Gleaner of Fredericton, but I am afraid I did not go about it in the right way. So, with the indulgence of the committee, I would like to read that article now because I think its terms will be helpful to the committee in considering the proposal I made.
William S. Fair, 23, came to Ottawa this week to see political leaders and government officials about his proposal that senior teen-agers be selected from each federal constituency to come to Ottawa and hold a mock parliamentary session.

The politicians and centennial planners see some merit in the idea from several angles-promoting good citizenship, giving young people a special role of their own in the centennial and marking the 100th birthday of confederation.
However, the politicians and some of the centennial planners also see in Mr. Fair's plan some political pitfalls.
For one thing they wouldn't be entirely happy about having the members of the youth parliament chosen in election contests with parties run under the labels of national political bodies. The planners would be fearful of having such organizations as the youth branches of the Liberal, Conservative, New Democratic and Social Credit parties take over.
I should like to say, as an aside at this point, that I would quite agree with them.
One suggestion is that elections might be held on the basis of new, fictitious parties, or parties not now active in national political affairs.
Another point of concern is: What would the youth parliament debate? What bills might it pass? What stands might it take which might prove to be distinctly embarrassing to the government of the day in 1967?
The politicians expect another general election to be held between now and the centennial year- or, if not, in 1967 itself.
Ottawa feels the project will need the sponsorship of some national body, such as a service club with branches in all federal ridings, to handle financing and organization.
It will also need endorsation by the government and the national centennial planners. Mr. Fair has suggested that Prince Charles might open the youth parliament session in the Senate chamber -as his mother did with the Canadian parliament in 1957-and that the sessions be held in the Commons chamber.
Though it is obvious that the suggestions made in this newspaper article are merely flying kites, I think they are worth quoting in connection with what I said earlier, because the article does give some idea of the objections which might be raised as well as some indication of what might be done in order to make the plan efficient and successful.
I appreciate the observation by the President of the Privy Council that it is intended to make the centenary celebration as widespread as possible. In this connection, a youth parliament, with its membership drawn from all parts of Canada, would seem eminently to fulfil that objective.

I listened very carefully to what was said by the President of the Privy Council as he outlined various projects planned to celebrate Canada's centennial which are now being considered, or which are under way. I should like the hon. gentleman to know that I, along with I believe most members of this group, would support many of the general proposals he has mentioned, and even a number of the specific undertakings to which he referred, including the restoration of the confederation buildings in Charlottetown, the building of some type of centre in Quebec city
Supply-Privy Council to commemorate the conference which was held there, and so on.
However, I am a little concerned about the omission of any special project to commemorate the date when two of the most important provinces in Canada actually entered confederation. I refer to 1905 when Alberta and Saskatchewan came in. There are other dates, of course-the dates when British Columbia and Manitoba joined confederation. I would think that on Canada's 100th birthday some consideration might be given to special projects commemorating these dates. I did not come prepared with any suggestions, but these came to mind while I was listening to the minister's remarks. Perhaps the federal government could undertake to build a second trans-Canada highway through these provinces and call it confederation highway. Or the federal government could undertake to build a large storage dam in the upper reaches of the South Saskatchewan river, a dam which would be a benefit to all the provinces of western Canada. I bring this up because there seems to be a lack of any provision to commemorate the dates when these other provinces came into confederation.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
The report will be, by reason of the hour, relatively brief. These estimates, as members of the committee know, were prepared a year ago. They appear as a section of the privy council office estimates contained in three votes, numbers 15, 20 and 25. In the meantime, the present government arranged for the emergency measures organization to become a separate agency responsible through its own deputy head to me as minister. At the same time, the administration of the civil defence college at Arnprior was transferred to the emergency measures organization. Since estimates for the college had been prepared by the Department of National Health and Welfare, it was deemed appropriate for the minister of that department to deal with those estimates for this year.
The objectives of civil emergency planning may be put as follows:
1.	To aid our people directly and through measures taken by government at all levels better to endure the effects of nuclear war, if it should occur, so that greater numbers would survive and more of the necessary items of supply remain to meet their needs.
2.	To add to the capability of Canada to meet the requirements of a modern conventional war, remembering that such a war may well place extremely severe and unique demands upon all of us and that, among other unusual conditions, there would always be the possibility of rapid escalation into nuclear war.
3.	To reduce as far as possible the losses in life and property occurring because of natural disasters affecting Canada.
In the period since I have been responsible for this work I have had some opportunity to review it. One is impressed with the marked advance in civil emergency planning in the last few years made by the provinces of Canada. Several of them have given it attention to a degree quite unknown before. They tend to stress the need to prepare for
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
natural disasters as well as for the major hazards of a possible war. They agree that these are all risks that we must recognize and that this sort of insurance is but prudent.
Vote 15 covers administrative costs of the emergency measures organization. The total staff is modest in size, numbering at present less than 100 persons, including the staff of the ten regional offices. Vote 20 includes the program for the provision of radiac instruments to measure wartime fallout and to enable forecasts to be made of impending danger to the people from this hazard. This is a program of shared costs with the provinces. Vote 25 reflects the importance of provincial and local government programs in civil emergency planning. It provides for federal financial assistance to provinces and municipalities up to 75 per cent of their costs.
Civil emergency planning, at least at the modest degree and at the level of costs we have provided in Canada, appears to be sensible. The Cuban crisis last year emphasized fully the need for instantly available emergency measures at such a time. Continued attention is required as part of our national and international effort. Civil emergency planning is part of our total defence. It merits a suitable portion of our attention, effort and money.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is indeed a brief report on a very important field of activity, but I think the house is glad to have had a report. Emergency measures work in Canada has now been going on for about 13 years and, as the minister pointed out, with increased emphasis during the last several years. The response by the provinces is very gratifying indeed. According to the latest issue of the emergency measures digest, as it is called, quite a substantial number of people have received training in various aspects of survival operations, which is very much to the good. The more widely knowledge is spread with regard to survival operations the better because, as the minister pointed out in a speech he made in October, some sentences of which he could have repeated here, we have to be on our guard. I am going to repeat two or three of those sentences which are taken from an address by the minister in October, 1963. He said:
There is no guarantee, whatever we may hope, that the present mild international climate will not degenerate again into freezing weather, with or without warning. Nuclear war remains a possibility, a remote one perhaps but nevertheless a worrisome one; and as long as this condition persists, we must continue the effort to improve our chances of surviving. In short, the civil emergency preparedness program is an insurance policy. As with other forms of insurance, there will be no regrets if we never collect on the policy...

That is a quotation with which I am thoroughly in accord. This is a form of national insurance. It is a field of activity in which every Canadian should be interested. I do not think we should take the point of view that nothing can be done in the event of nuclear war. I think that is wrong. I do not think we should take the point of view that civil defence measures are an indication that a nation can endure a nuclear war. I heard that doctrine advanced just the other day. I think that is wrong. I think it is just sound common sense to be prepared for emergencies. We do so through our defence operations in order that if conventional or nuclear war breaks out we will have forces ready to take action; but under modern conditions the civil population must be prepared for survival operations, even if it is a war after the fashion of the second world war, with the awful destruction that was caused just by the conventional weapons of that period.
So it is sound common sense to have an emergency measures program, and even if it has not gone too well in some areas this is no excuse for not continuing the program on a national scale and with the co-operation of the provinces. A debt of gratitude is due to those people, the director and his staff, who have carried on during the past several years without any particular public recognition or any particular blare of trumpets, because this is a field of activity in which some people are interested and some are not. Nevertheless it is vital to Canada's welfare and I hope that it will continue without abatement so that we are ready for any emergency whatsoever.
I have one note that is not quite in keeping with all that has gone before. I had an argument with the Minister of National Defence as to the role of the militia with regard to this particular problem, and I presume I will have to wait until he reappears with his estimates to conclude that debate. I think he suggested that the minister reporting for emergency measures might have something to say about the role of the militia, but I would prefer to have it right from the mouth of the Minister of National Defence himself; so I will not press the minister, who perhaps has too many other things to do than to carry part of the burden for the Minister of National Defence.
Item agreed to.
